chains.title: GABPA/ETS site creation at the TERT promoter

links.claim: GABPA binds the alt A allele more strongly than ref G at this base. GABPA's own QBiC-SELEX model gives effect +4.01, z 68.47, above the gate, and E17 reports a mapped ETS model with effect +2.121, z 166.19, also alt-binding; the alt site reaches a strong percentile. GABPA is the best-supported ETS candidate because it is expressed in glioblastoma at 15.52 TPM, has ENCODE ChIP peaks over this base only in non-matching biosamples HepG2 and SK-N-SH, and literature identifies GABPA/GABP tetramers at mutant TERT promoter ETS motifs. ETV2, ETV3 and FLI1 share an ETS model but have unknown occupancy and lower expression. No glioblastoma ENCODE GABPA peak over this base is shown, so disease-context occupancy is inferred rather than directly demonstrated.
The variant lies in promoter-like cCRE EH38E3622530, a PLS at the TERT upstream promoter with active promoter chromatin marks DNase, H3K27ac and H3K4me3.
The element is 0.0 kb from the TERT transcription start site and is annotated as a TERT upstream/promoter variant; TERT is the nearest gene.

TERT promoter mutations and GABPA/GABPB1-dependent TERT activation are established in glioblastoma and bladder cancer; TERT is also relevant in melanoma, although melanoma-specific GABPA evidence at this base is limited.

Alt A is predicted to strengthen a GABPA/ETS site and increase TERT transcription and telomerase, promoting tumor maintenance or progression. This is supported by GABP-dependent activation of mutant TERT promoters and by GABPA/GABPB1 knockdown inhibiting telomerase and tumorigenicity in glioblastoma, but no supplied evidence tests this exact allele's effect on TERT expression, telomerase or disease.

predictions: Allele-specific GABPA ChIP at this base shows higher GABPA occupancy on alt A than ref G in a TERT-expressing glioblastoma line heterozygous at the variant.
An isolated alt-A vs ref-G TERT reporter, or endogenous knock-in, increases TERT mRNA or telomerase activity; GABPA or GABPB1 knockdown reduces the alt-specific increase.
The alt allele retains an effect after controlling for linked canonical TERT promoter mutations and tracks with GABPA/GABPB1 dependence.
falsified_if: No alt-specific GABPA occupancy is detected at this base in a TERT-expressing glioblastoma, melanoma or bladder cancer cell line.
Isolated alt A vs ref G does not change TERT reporter, mRNA or telomerase activity when linked variants are controlled.
GABPA or GABPB1 knockdown, or ETS-motif disruption, does not reduce the alt-specific TERT signal.

chains.title: TFAP2A loss-of-repressor at the TERT promoter

links.claim: TFAP2A binds the ref G allele more strongly than alt A in QBiC-SELEX: effect -1.289, z -36.84, above the gate, with a strong site. TFAP2A is expressed at 9.65 TPM in glioblastoma; TFAP2C shares the same AP-2 model and is lower expressed. Neither has ENCODE occupancy over this base, so this is a motif-based candidate with unknown occupancy.
The variant lies in the active TERT promoter PLS EH38E3622530, so an AP-2 site change could in principle affect promoter activity.
The element is at the TERT transcription start site, making TERT the direct candidate target gene.
TERT is relevant in glioblastoma, melanoma and bladder cancer, but there is no TFAP2A-specific disease evidence for this base.

Speculative only: if TFAP2A represses TERT, the alt A allele would reduce TFAP2A binding, relieve repression and increase TERT. No supplied evidence shows TFAP2A represses TERT or that this allele changes TERT expression or disease.

predictions: Ref G shows more TFAP2A ChIP at this base than alt A in a TFAP2A-expressing disease-relevant cell line.
If TFAP2A represses TERT, alt A should de-repress TERT and increase TERT reporter or mRNA; TFAP2A overexpression should lower TERT more strongly on ref G than on alt A.
TFAP2A knockdown should increase TERT expression at this promoter.
falsified_if: TFAP2A does not occupy the TERT promoter at this base in disease-relevant cells.
Alt A does not change TERT expression or telomerase activity.
TFAP2A does not repress TERT in reporter assays, or TFAP2A knockdown does not increase TERT.

chains.title: CTCF loss at an insulator/architectural site

links.claim: CTCF binds the ref G allele more strongly than alt A in QBiC-SELEX: effect -1.719, z -14.7, above the gate, with a strong site. CTCF is expressed at 26.45 TPM in glioblastoma and has one ENCODE peak over this variant only in DOHH2, not in a matching disease context; the cCRE has only a low CTCF z-score of 2.0. This is a motif-based candidate without disease-relevant occupancy.
The variant lies in the TERT promoter PLS with low CTCF cCRE signal and a predicted CTCF site change, but an insulator or architectural function at this promoter is not established.

The element is at the TERT transcription start site, so altered CTCF binding could in principle affect TERT promoter contacts, but no supplied evidence shows CTCF-dependent TERT regulation at this base.
TERT is relevant in glioblastoma, melanoma and bladder cancer, but there is no CTCF-specific disease evidence for this base.

Speculative only: alt A would reduce CTCF binding and potentially disrupt a promoter-proximal insulator or chromatin contact, permitting increased TERT expression. No supplied evidence shows altered CTCF binding, chromatin contacts, TERT expression, telomerase activity or disease for this allele.

predictions: Ref G shows more CTCF ChIP at this base than alt A in a CTCF-expressing disease-relevant cell line.
Alt A reduces CTCF binding and alters TERT promoter-enhancer contacts or chromatin architecture.
CTCF depletion mimics the alt A allele's effect on TERT expression.
falsified_if: CTCF does not occupy this base in disease-relevant cells.
Alt A does not change CTCF binding or TERT promoter-enhancer contacts.
CTCF depletion does not mimic the alt allele's effect on TERT.

grades_v0.reason: QBiC-SELEX supports an alt-specific ETS/ETV5-like motif change, but the only ChIP evidence over this base is from non-matching biosamples (HepG2, SK-N-SH). E04 explicitly says no ENCODE biosample matches the glioblastoma expression context, so occupancy in the disease context is inferred, not shown.
E03 places the variant inside promoter-like cCRE EH38E3622530 with DNase, H3K27ac and H3K4me3 signal, and E01 annotates it as an ENSR5_832QG promoter upstream of TERT.
E02 places TERT 0.0 kb from its TSS and E01 annotates the variant as TERT upstream_gene_variant, directly supporting the gene assignment.

E15 is only a broad Europe PMC search with titles, not variant-specific evidence. It is consistent with TERT relevance in melanoma and glioblastoma, but it does not directly establish TERT promoter activity or mutation relevance in all listed diseases, and bladder evidence is absent from the listed hits.

E17 supports only an in vitro binding change. No cited evidence shows that this allele increases TERT transcription, telomerase activity, or tumor phenotype, and E15 gives no variant-specific functional result.

QBiC-SELEX supports ref-allele binding for TFAP2A, but TFAP2A was never assayed by ENCODE at this base and has no ChIP occupancy over the variant in a relevant cell type. A QBiC-SELEX change alone is at best weak support for a binding link.
E03 and E01 directly place the variant in the active TERT promoter PLS. The AP-2 functional consequence remains inferential, but the element-location claim is directly supported.
E02 and E01 directly place the element at the TERT TSS and annotate TERT as the nearest/upstream gene.
E15 is a broad literature search rather than direct evidence for this variant or for the full glioblastoma/melanoma/bladder disease set. It is consistent but indirect.
The repressor mechanism and the alt-allele de-repression effect on TERT are explicitly stated as plausible but not directly supported; no evidence IDs are supplied for this phenotype link.

QBiC-SELEX supports ref-allele binding for CTCF, and E13 reports one ChIP peak only in DOHH2. There is no CTCF occupancy over this base in the glioblastoma expression context, so the binding link is not supported.

E03 places the variant in a PLS and reports low CTCF cCRE z-score, and E19 gives a predicted CTCF site change. This is consistent with a possible architectural role but does not demonstrate an insulator or architectural function at this promoter.
E02 and E01 support TERT TSS proximity, but no cited evidence shows that altered CTCF binding at this base affects TERT promoter contacts or transcription.
E15 is a broad, indirect literature search and does not directly establish TERT promoter relevance for this variant across the listed diseases.

The phenotype claim depends on an assumed insulator/architectural mechanism and reduced CTCF binding increasing TERT. E19 and E03 provide motif and cCRE context only; no evidence shows altered TERT expression, telomerase activity, or chromatin contacts.

grades_final.reason: QBiC-SELEX supports an alt-gained ETS/GABPA site (E17, E33), but the only ENCODE GABPA occupancy over this base is in HepG2/SK-N-SH, not glioblastoma (E32); no matching-cell-type ChIP or allele-specific occupancy is shown. The GABPA choice among ETS factors is literature-motivated, but occupancy at this exact base in disease context remains inferred.
E03 directly places the variant in PLS EH38E3622530 with promoter chromatin marks, and E01 annotates a TERT promoter regulatory feature.
E02 places TERT at 0.0 kb from its TSS and E01 annotates the variant as a TERT upstream/promoter variant.

E34k directly states that GABPA/GABPB1 activate mutant TERT promoters in glioblastoma and bladder cancer; E34f adds glioblastoma support. Melanoma TERT relevance is less direct but the claim explicitly limits this.

Evidence supports GABP-dependent activation of other mutant TERT promoters and GABPA/GABPB1 knockdown effects, but no supplied assay tests this exact alt allele's effect on TERT expression, telomerase, or tumor phenotype. The phenotype direction is inferred from SELEX plus literature, not directly demonstrated.

QBiC-SELEX shows ref allele binding more strongly for TFAP2A/AP-2 models (E30, E31), but neither TF has ENCODE occupancy over this base; this is a motif-based binding prediction only, with no occupancy evidence.
E03/E01 place the variant in an active TERT promoter PLS, so the element context for a possible AP-2 site effect is directly supported.
E02/E01 directly identify TERT as the nearest gene at the TSS; no evidence supports a different target.

TERT relevance in glioblastoma/melanoma/bladder is supported (E15, E34k), but the cited evidence gives no TFAP2A-specific disease or cell-type evidence at this promoter. The claim itself acknowledges this absence, so the link is only indirect for TFAP2A.
No evidence is cited for TFAP2A repressing TERT or for this allele changing TERT expression; the phenotype is explicitly speculative.

QBiC-SELEX shows ref allele binding more strongly for CTCF (E19), but the only ENCODE CTCF peak over the variant is in DOHH2 (E13), not a disease-relevant cell type; cCRE CTCF signal is low (E03). Binding is motif-based only.

E03 places the variant in a PLS with low CTCF z-score and E19 predicts a CTCF site change, but no evidence establishes insulator or architectural function at this promoter. The element is a promoter, while the CTCF architectural role is speculative.

E02/E01 support TERT as the nearest gene at the TSS, but the claim that altered CTCF binding could affect TERT promoter contacts is unsupported; no CTCF-dependent TERT regulation at this base is shown.
TERT disease relevance is supported (E15), but there is no CTCF-specific disease or cell-type evidence for this base; the link does not establish CTCF function in the claimed context.
No evidence is cited for altered CTCF binding, chromatin contacts, TERT expression, telomerase activity, or disease for this allele; the phenotype is explicitly speculative.

Candidates are TFs whose ENCODE ChIP-seq peaks contain the variant and that are expressed (DepMap subtype median Glioblastoma), bound here before bound elsewhere, then a strong site before a weak one, then by |z|; then expressed TFs ENCODE never assayed whose best model passes the gate (occupancy unknown). Shown: 10 of 20 occupied (15 with a strong site), 5 of 111 with unknown occupancy. Left out: 0 TFs assayed in the matching biosample and 552 assayed only elsewhere, none with a peak here; 1 bound but below 1 TPM. The gate (|z| > 4.05, Bonferroni over 997 models) marks a change QBiC-SELEX detects; it says nothing about occupancy. Effect > 0 means the alternate allele binds more strongly. In vitro binding only. Site strength is the better allele's best k-mer over the variant, as a percentile of the best model's k-mers; a strong site reaches the 97.5th. Telomere length maintenance, critical for cancer progression, can be driven by TERT promoter mutations (TERTp MUT ), which are markers of poor prognosis across multiple cancers.

Here, we identified previously uncharacterized pathways regulating TERTp MUT activity by inserting a luciferase reporter downstream of TERTp MUT in SW1736 anaplastic thyroid cancer cells via CRISPR-Cas9, generating SW1736TERT/LUC, and screening a 218-kinase inhibitor library.
TERT promoter (TERTp) mutations create a de novo E26 transformation-specific (ETS) transcription factor binding motif.
Here, we analyzed 53 cell lines representing 16 cancer types and 6 recurrent TERTp mutations and found that the GA-binding protein (GABP) tetramer is responsible for promoter activation in all cases.
Beyond the two most common point mutations, which selectively recruit the ETS factor GABP to activate TERT, the significance of other variants is unknown.

The duplications recruit a GABP tetramer by virtue of the native ETS motif and its precisely spaced duplicated counterpart, activate the promoter and are clonal in a TERT expressing multifocal glioblastoma.
They generate a novel Ets/TCF binding site.
We compared sense and antisense transcription of a panel of TERT promoter-luciferase vectors harboring the -124C>T and -146C>T mutations alone or together.

We detect hundreds to thousands of allele-specific chromatin accessibility variants (ASCAVs) in each melanoma genome, of which 15%-20% can be explained by gains or losses of transcription factor binding sites.
Finally, by augmenting the DeepMEL2 model with ChIP-seq data for GABPA, the TERT promoter mutation, as well as additional ETS motif gains, can be identified with high confidence.

TERT promoter mutations occur in the majority of glioblastoma, bladder cancer (BC), and other malignancies while the ETS family transcription factors GABPA and its partner GABPB1 activate the mutant TERT promoter and telomerase in these tumors.
GABPA depletion or the disruption of the GABPA/GABPB1 complex by knocking down GABPB1 was shown to inhibit telomerase, thereby eliminating the tumorigenic potential of glioblastoma cells.
